## Background

There are many *graphic systems* in R for making plots and figures. These include **"base R graphics"** like the `plot()` and add on packages like **ggplot2**

Let's compare how we make a simple graph with these two systems:

We can use the in-built `cars` dataset:

```{r}
head(cars)
```

a base R plot:

```{r}
plot(cars)
```

Now for **ggplot2** 
Before I can use ggplot2 I need to install it on my computer.To do this we can use t function `install.packages("ggplot2)`


**Note** We never run an `install.packages()` in our quarto doc ( we run it in our R console) as it would re-install the package every time I render my document

Once installed we still need to load up the package into our R session. We do this with a `library()` call

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(cars)
```

Every ggplot needs at least 3 inputs: 

- the **data** (a data.frame of the stuff we want to plot)
- the **aesthetics** (how the data maps to the plot)
- the **geom** layer (how you want the plot drawn)

```{r}
ggplot(cars) + 
  aes(x = speed, y = dist) +
  geom_point()
```

## Lets add some features (more layers)

Let's add a trend line that shows the relationship between `speed` and `distance`

```{r}
ggplot(cars) +
  aes(x = speed, y = dist)+
  geom_point() + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "Speed (MPH)", y = "Stopping distance (FT)", title = "Stopping distance of some old cars")
```

## Gene Expression Plot

First we will read some expression data for the effects of a GLP-1 drug

```{r}
url <- "https://bioboot.github.io/bimm143_S20/class-material/up_down_expression.txt"
genes <- read.delim(url)
head(genes)
```

```{r}
p <- ggplot(genes) + 
  aes(x = Condition1, y = Condition2, col = State) +
  geom_point() 
p
p + scale_colour_manual( values=c("blue","gray","red") ) +
  labs(x = "Control", y = "Drug Treatment", title = "GLP-1 inhibitor effects on gene expression")
```

Q. Use the colnames() function and the ncol() function on the genes data frame to find out what the column names are (we will need these later) and how many columns there are. How many columns did you find?

```{r}
colnames(genes)
ncol(genes)
```

Q. Use the table() function on the State column of this data.frame to find out how many ‘up’ regulated genes there are. What is your answer?

```{r}
table(genes$State)
```

Q. Using your values above and 2 significant figures. What fraction of total genes is up-regulated in this dataset?

```{r}
n.total <- nrow(genes)
n.up <- genes$State == "up"
UP <- sum(n.up)
Total <- sum(n.total)
fraction <- UP/Total
fraction
round(fraction, 2)
```

## Going Further

```{r}
url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jennybc/gapminder/master/inst/extdata/gapminder.tsv"
gapminder <- read.delim(url)
#install.packages("dplyr")
head(gapminder)
```

Q: how many entries in this dataset
```{r}
nrow(gapminder)
```
Q: how many different country values?

```{r}
length(table(gapminder$country))
```

```{r}
unique(gapminder$country)
```

First Plot of `gdpPercap` vs `lifeExp`:

```{r}
ggplot(gapminder) +
  geom_point()+
  aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, col = continent)+
  labs( x= "GDP Per Capita", y = "Life Expectancy", Title = "Relationship between GDP Per Capita and Life Expectancy")
```

One useful layer we can add to explore big datasets like this is called "facetting"

```{r}
ggplot(gapminder) +
  geom_point()+
  facet_wrap(~continent)+
  aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, col = continent)+
  labs( x= "GDP Per Capita", y = "Life Expectancy", Title = "Relationship between GDP Per Capita and Life Expectancy")
```

### limit to 1977 and 2007
we can install **dplyr** package to help us "filter" the full dataset down to a smaller subset that only includes the years we want
```{r}
#gapminder$year
library(dplyr)
filter(gapminder, year == 2007, country == "India")
```
